TAVI-related conduction disturbances Acquired conduction disturbances after TAVI are frequent and may lead to heart failure (re-) admissions and impaired long-term prognosis18-22. The atrioventricular bundle pierces the membranous septum between the right and non-coronary cusp of the aortic valve and surfaces along the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT), which makes it vulnerable to contact pressure by the implanted transcatheter heart valve (THV) during TAVI23, 24. New left bundle branch block (LBBB) and third-degree atrioventricular block (AV3B) requiring PPI occur in up to a third and quarter of patients, respectively18-22. These conduction disturbances may be transient or remain permanent which is clinically relevant in view of in-hospital stay and overall healthcare costs. Unfortunately, there are no uniform definitions to describe conduction dynamics post-TAVI. Inconsistent reporting makes the interpretation of the literature on this topic challenging. Part III of this thesis will elaborate on what is currently known about the incidence of newly acquired conduction disturbances after TAVI and studies specific features on the baseline and postprocedural electrocardiogram (ECG) to predict conduction dynamics. These insights may help determine the need and timing of PPI and adjust hospital discharge policies.

title: Impact of Balloon Post-Dilatation Strategy During Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation on the Cardiac Conduction System
authors: Ekrem Şahan; Süleyman Kalaycı; Suzan Şahan; Orhan Maden
abstract: BACKGROUND: Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has become a well-established treatment for patients with severe aortic stenosis who are at intermediate or high surgical risk. Despite procedural advances, post-procedural conduction disturbances remain among the most common complications, particularly new-onset left bundle branch block (LBBB). This study aimed to investigate the impact of balloon pre- and post-dilatation on the cardiac conduction system during TAVI. METHOD: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 447 consecutive patients who underwent successful TAVI between June 2021 and June 2025. After excluding patients with baseline bundle branch block or permanent pacemaker rhythm, 282 patients were included. Standard 12-lead electrocardiograms were evaluated before and after TAVI. Post-procedural QRS prolongation was defined as QRS >120 ms, and logistic regression analysis was performed to identify predictors. RESULT: The mean age was 76.5 ± 6.9 years, and 63.8% of patients were female. Larger prosthesis diameter (OR = 1.173, 95% CI 1.082-1.271; P < .001) and post-dilatation (OR = 2.147, 95% CI 1.235-3.733; P = .007) were independently associated with QRS prolongation. Post-dilatation specifically correlated with new-onset LBBB but not with right bundle branch block (RBBB), intraventricular conduction delay, or high-grade atrioventricular (AV) block. No significant predictors were identified for permanent pacemaker implantation. CONCLUSION: Balloon post-dilatation during TAVI is an independent risk factor for the development of new-onset LBBB. Patients with pre-existing conduction abnormalities, such as RBBB or first-degree AVr block, should be monitored closely after post-dilatation, as LBBB may adversely affect left ventricular function and long-term clinical outcomes.

title: Direct Vision Cardiac Surgery via Minimal Lateral Thoracotomy: Which Procedure is it Most Suitable for?
authors: Yasin Özden; Ege Seferoglu; Mutlu Şenocak; Yavuz Şensöz; İlyas Kayacıoğlu
abstract: Introduction: Minimal approaches have become popular in cardiac surgery in recent years worldwide; as in other surgical specialties, minimal right anterior thoracotomy (RAT) and minimal right lateral thoracotomy (RLT) techniques can be used for some cardiac procedures.This study compares and presents the operative and postoperative advantages and disadvantages of both techniques.Methods: Between March 2021 and July 2024, a total of 40 patients underwent cardiac surgery via direct vision minimally invasive right thoracotomy approach at Cardiovascular Surgery Center of University of Health Sciences Türkiye, Dr. Siyami Ersek Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery Training and Research Hospital.Eight of these patients underwent surgery with the RAT technique, and 32 underwent surgery with the RLT technique.Operative and postoperative outcomes were compared.Results: One patient who underwent RAT died during the operative period, and two patients who underwent RLT died during the postoperative period.Cross-clamp and cardiopulmonary bypass times were longer for RAT during the operative period.While there was no difference in extubation times or intensive care stay durations, tube drainage times and hospital stays were shorter for RLT in the postoperative period.Conclusion: These findings suggest a potential clinical advantage of direct-vision RLT; however, they require further validation in large-scale, prospective studies.The situation may be different in camera-assisted approaches.

title: Study on the construction and application effect of discharge preparation services in heart valve replacement surgery
authors: Chunyan Zhang; Huan Yu; Wei Zhai; Lili Zhang; Ting Zhang; 李媛媛
abstract: Objective To develop and evaluate a discharge preparation service (DPS) for patients after heart valve replacement surgery. Method This retrospective cohort study included 323 patients who underwent heart valve replacement surgery between February 2023 and January 2025. A multidisciplinary DPS plan was developed using a modified Delphi method and implemented in clinical practice. After 1:1 propensity score matching, 110 patients receiving DPS and 110 receiving usual care were analyzed. RHDS and QDTS were assessed at discharge; CSMS, CCQQ, and NSNS were assessed at discharge and at 3 and 6 months after discharge. Linear mixed models examined time, group, and time × group interactions. Results All items in the DPS plan were agreed upon by experts (average importance score ≥4.0, coefficient of variation ≤0.25), with a Kendall's coefficient of concordance W value of 0.925 ( P < 0.001), and the expert authority coefficient was 0.914. After propensity score matching (PSM), there were no significant differences in baseline characteristics between the two groups ( P > 0.05, standardized mean difference <0.1). Compared with controls, the DPS group had significantly higher RHDS and QDTS scores at discharge ( P < 0.05). For CSMS, CCQQ, and NSNS, time × group interactions were significant [CSMS: F(2,436) = 77.73; CCQQ: F(2,436) = 93.92; NSNS: F(2,436) = 67.53; all P < 0.001], indicating steeper improvement trajectories with DPS. At 6 months after discharge, the interaction estimates were 11.23 (95% CI 9.23–13.23) for CSMS, 15.61 (95% CI 13.36–17.86) for CCQQ, and 10.40 (95% CI 8.60–12.20) for NSNS (all P < 0.001). DPS was associated with lower unplanned readmission (6.36% vs. 15.45%, P = 0.031) and lower total complications (25.45% vs. 59.09%, P < 0.001). Conclusion The systematic, multidisciplinary DPS plan was associated with significant improvements in discharge readiness, self-management ability, and quality of life, as well as lower rates of unplanned readmissions and complications after heart valve replacement surgery.

title: Beyond the trigger: the unknown precipitant as a high-risk phenotype in acute heart failure
authors: Georgios Aletras; Maria Bachlitzanaki; M Stratinaki; Emmanuel Lamprogiannakis; Emmanuel Foukarakis; Yannis Pantazis; Michalis Hamilos; Kostas Stylianou
abstract: Background A substantial proportion of patients with acute heart failure (AHF) present without an identifiable precipitating factor. We compared the clinical profile, echocardiographic characteristics, and mid-term outcomes of AHF patients stratified by precipitating factor category. Methods We conducted a prospective single-center observational study at Venizelio General Hospital, Heraklion, including 486 consecutive patients hospitalized with AHF between February 2023 and January 2025. Patients were classified into three groups: behavioral ( n = 148), non-behavioral/clinical ( n = 230), and unknown ( n = 108). The primary endpoint was all-cause death at 12 months; secondary endpoints were terminal renal replacement therapy (RRT) and a composite of death, AHF rehospitalization or RRT. Groups were compared by Kaplan–Meier analysis and Cox regression with the behavioral group as reference, and the cumulative incidence of first AHF rehospitalization was estimated with death and terminal RRT as competing events. Results The unknown group was older and more frail (CFS ≥5), with more advanced chronic kidney disease, more right heart failure and lower TAPSE, higher NT-proBNP and lower admission eGFR. All-cause mortality at 12 months was 41.7% versus 20.3% and 29.6% (log-rank p < 0.001; unknown vs. behavioral HR 2.44, 95% CI 1.54–3.88), with a parallel gradient for the composite endpoint (event-free survival 35.2% vs. 58.8% and 52.6%; HR 1.96, 1.39–2.77). After adjustment for age, admission eGFR, right heart failure, NT-proBNP and frailty, precipitant category no longer improved model fit (likelihood ratio p = 0.066) and the association of the unknown group with mortality was attenuated and no longer significant (adjusted HR 1.43, 0.88–2.31). With death and terminal RRT as competing events, 12-month cumulative incidence of first AHF rehospitalization did not differ (36.1% vs. 29.7% and 26.1%; p = 0.207). ACEi/ARB prescription at discharge was lower in the unknown group (21.2% vs. 39.0% and 44.2%, p < 0.001). Conclusions In AHF, the absence of an identifiable precipitating factor identifies a high-risk phenotype characterized by advanced multimorbidity, right ventricular dysfunction, renal impairment and worse mid-term outcomes. The difference was driven predominantly by mortality rather than rehospitalization, and the association was attenuated after adjustment for the phenotype-defining variables. The label may therefore serve as an early bedside marker of advanced disease, requiring confirmation in multicenter cohorts.

title: New surgical technique for repairing ALCAPA originating from the non-facing pulmonary sinus: The Aswan Drawbridge technique
authors: Amr Alsalakawy; Ahmed Mahgoub; Amr Elsawy; Islam Rashwan; Mohamed Adel; Ahmed Afifi; Hatem Hosny; Magdi Habib Yacoub
abstract: Background: Anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA) is a rare congenital anomaly in which coronary steal causes progressive left ventricular ischemia, dysfunction, and secondary mitral regurgitation. Direct reimplantation into the aorta is the gold standard. However, it is technically hazardous when the left coronary artery (LCA) arises from the distant non-facing pulmonary sinus, because tension on the transferred vessel risks occluding it. The Takeuchi procedure is an established alternative, but it has limitations, particularly when the anomalous ostium lies close to a pulmonary valve commissure.Technique: We describe the “Aswan Drawbridge” technique in an asymptomatic 8-year-old girl whose anomalous LCA ostium lay immediately adjacent to a pulmonary valve commissure. The commissure was partially detached to maximize the harvested coronary button. A long aortic flap was then created in the left coronary sinus and reflected inferiorly, like a drawbridge, to form the floor of the tunnel. The lateral flaps of the button were sutured to this aortic flap, creating a tension-free tunnel of autologous arterial tissue between the LCA and the aorta. The pulmonary artery defect was reconstructed with an autologous pericardial patch, and the detached commissure was resuspended to it.Outcome: The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 7. Cardiac computed tomography at 1 month showed a patent 5-mm tunnel without kinking, stenosis, or compression. At 3 years, the patient remained asymptomatic, with normal biventricular function and regression of mitral regurgitation from moderate to mild, consistent with left ventricular reverse remodeling.Conclusion: The Aswan Drawbridge technique is a feasible option for ALCAPA arising from the non-facing pulmonary sinus. Longer follow-up is needed to establish the tunnel’s durability.

title: Comparison of 1-year costs of commercially insured patients with severe aortic stenosis undergoing surgical vs. transcatheter aortic valve replacement
authors: Suzanne J. Baron; Benjamin Zev Galper; Marcella A. Kelley; Soumya G. Chikermane; Shannon M. E. Murphy
abstract: Patients with aortic stenosis (AS) have been shown to have lower costs at 1 year with transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) compared with surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) in a Medicare population. The difference in costs between TAVR and SAVR in commercially insured patients with AS in the United States is unknown. Using the Optum claims database, AS patients receiving either TAVR or SAVR between 3/2019 and 9/2022 were identified. Patients were categorized into low, intermediate or high strata using the Hospital Frailty Risk Score (HFRS). The primary outcome was total 1-year cost, defined as the sum of index AVR hospitalization and 1-year follow-up costs. Risk-adjusted generalized linear models were used to assess the difference in the costs between TAVR and SAVR. 3,623 patients (952 TAVR; 2,671 SAVR) were identified. TAVR patients had lower index hospitalization costs compared with SAVR patients across all HFRS strata (cost difference for low: $39,312, p < 0.01; intermediate: $42,006, p < 0.01; high: $39,431, p = 0.03). Cumulative costs through one year were significantly lower with TAVR in the low and intermediate HFRS strata (cost difference for low: $32,116, p < 0.01; intermediate $40,905, p < 0.01) and numerically lower in the high HFRS stratum (cost difference: $35,881, p = 0.15). When the analysis was restricted to isolated AVR, the 1-year difference was no longer significant in the low and intermediate HFRS strata ($8,064 and $11,314, respectively) and was numerically reversed in the high HFRS stratum (−$28,804). In a commercial payor population of real-world patients with AS, TAVR was associated with lower standardized index hospitalization costs across all HFRS strata and lower standardized 1-year costs in the low and intermediate HFRS strata. These findings demonstrate that baseline frailty and procedural scope are critical determinants of short and intermediate-term cost differences between TAVR and SAVR for the treatment of AS in commercial populations.

title: Angina Severity in Severe Aortic Stenosis with a Single Intermediate Left Anterior Descending Artery Lesion: Associations with Measured Aortic Valve Area and Epicardial Pressure-Derived Indices
authors: Artur Dziewierz; Barbara Zdzierak; Tomasz Rakowski; Łukasz Niewiara; Piotr Szolc; Jacek Legutko; Paweł Kleczyński
journal: Journal of Cardiovascular Development and Disease
abstract: Attributing exertional symptoms in patients with aortic stenosis (AS) and coronary artery disease is challenging. We performed a secondary analysis of a single-center prospective registry of 190 patients with severe high-gradient AS and a single intermediate left anterior descending lesion assessed with fractional flow reserve (FFR) and instantaneous wave-free ratio (iFR). The primary outcome was angina severity (Canadian Cardiovascular Society [CCS] class III–IV vs. II); New York Heart Association (NYHA) class III–IV vs. II functional limitation was secondary and exploratory. Among 185 complete cases, older age (odds ratio [OR] 3.00 per decade, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.84–4.87; p < 0.001) and smaller measured aortic valve area (AVA; OR 1.39 per 0.1 cm2 decrease, 95% CI 1.08–1.79; p = 0.009) were independently associated with severe angina, whereas lesion morphology, FFR, and iFR were not. No variable was independently associated with NYHA class III–IV limitation, although this analysis was underpowered. Because AVA is flow dependent and transvalvular flow and coronary microvascular function were not directly measured, the AVA association does not establish fixed valvular obstruction as the mechanism of angina. The lack of association with FFR/iFR pertains to symptom severity and does not invalidate their use for lesion-level hemodynamic assessment.

title: In Vivo Gene Editing of PCSK9 in the Prevention of Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease: From Genetic Validation to Clinical Application
authors: Pablo Corral; Natalia Nardelli
abstract: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) is the primary causal and modifiable risk factor.Available lipid-lowering therapies-statins, ezetimibe, anti-PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies, and RNA interference-have been shown to reduce cardiovascular events, but they require long-term administration and are limited by efficacy, adherence, cost, and access.Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is, to date, the most genetically validated target for the development of in vivo gene-editing strategies aimed at achieving a permanent reduction in LDL-C through a single therapeutic administration.This review describes the biology of PCSK9, the available gene-editing platforms-CRISPR-Cas9, base editing, and primer editing-and their delivery to hepatocytes via lipid nanoparticles.It summarizes preclinical data and ongoing clinical trials (VERVE-101, VERVE-102, and YOLT-101) showing sustained, dose-dependent reductions in LDL-C following a single infusion, with acceptable short-term safety profiles.Finally, the long-term safety, regulatory, economic, and ethical challenges that will determine the eventual translation of this technology into routine clinical practice are discussed.

title: A rare cause of dysfunction of mechanical aortic valve prosthesis in a young adult
authors: Todor Dimitrov; Ивилин Тодоров
abstract: A mechanical prosthetic valve dysfunction carries a high risk of hospitalization and patient death. It may show up as stenosis of the valve prosthesis or intra/paraprosthetic regurgitation. Prosthetic stenosis, in turn, may be caused by granulation tissue (pannus), thrombosis, a combination of pannus and thrombosis, a prosthesis mechanical defect, or a unique surgical technique. Establishing the specific cause of prosthetic stenosis is of crucial importance for the therapeutic behavior. Prosthetic thrombosis requires conservative intensification of anticoagulation/fibrinolysis or surgical treatment in an accelerated/emergency manner. When the cause of the thrombosis is pannus, a mechanical defect, or surgical technique, the only treatment option is cardiac surgical reintervention. The manifestation of granulation tissue (pannus) is indicative of a non-immune reaction to the prosthetic valve and suture material following prosthetic valve replacement. The basis of this phenomenon is the growth of fibroelastic tissue associated with an increase in the expression of transforming growth factor beta. [1] In a small proportion of patients with implanted prosthetic valves, the growth of pannus leads to subvalvular obstruction of blood flow and results in prosthetic stenosis. Despite the technological advancements in imaging diagnostics, visualizing pannus remains challenging and not always feasible. Consequently, we employ a multifaceted approach that incorporates anamnestic, clinical, and imaging methods to reach a diagnosis. Operative exploration is the only method by which definitive confirmation can be obtained. The objective of this article was twofold: first, to present a rare case of stenosis of a mechanical aortic valve prosthesis due to a circumferential shaft of granulation tissue (pannus) forming a kind of de novo subaortic membrane; and second, to outline an algorithm for the diagnosis of prosthetic valve stenosis and differential diagnosis between thrombosis and pannus as the cause of valve dysfunction. The following case study presents a patient who met the surgical treatment indications due to stenosis of a mechanical aortic valve prosthesis. The clinical information and imaging studies indicated that the prosthetic dysfunction was likely due to the presence of granulation tissue (pannus). The intraoperative finding revealed a circumferential shaft of granulation tissue, forming a novel subaortic membrane.

title: Performance of a foundation model to generate thousands of predicted outcomes across multiple use cases
authors: Matteo Mischiati; Kyriakos Vattis; Richard E Gliklich; Michelle B Leavy; Costas Boussios; Jigar N. Bandaria
abstract: Background. Predictive artificial intelligence (AI) models hold great promise for medical care. While many types of models have proliferated across healthcare and the life sciences, systematic, rapid generation of multi-condition predictions of diagnoses, future medical events and future clinical outcomes from a single foundation-model architecture remains rare. PhenOM® is a generative AI foundation model trained and validated on longitudinal medical-event data from more than 400 million patient records in the OM1 Real World Data Cloud (RWDC) and designed to complete predictive tasks for a broad array of medical diagnoses, events and clinical outcomes (collectively outcomes) at varying time intervals, currently up to five (5) years. This paper describes the implementation of PhenOM to complete a vast number of predictive tasks across clinical domains and outcomes. Methods. PhenOM was evaluated across four outcome categories (Future Risk, Screening, Care Opportunity, and Treatment Effect) in multiple domains spanning chronic disease, acute medical events, healthcare utilization, and rare and frequently undiagnosed conditions. Performance was assessed using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Outcomes were defined within an eligible-population framework using standardized medical code sets (ICD-10, SNOMED, CPT, NDC, LOINC) unless outcomes could not be specified with an existing code. All benchmarks reported were derived from data excluded from training. Results. As of this publication, the single PhenOM model has been used to complete and validate thousands of predictive tasks covering more than 1,770 outcomes spanning most organ systems and clinical specialties, with new predictive tasks being validated each day. Overall, 80 percent of predictive tasks achieved AUROC of at least 0.70 and 30 percent achieved AUROC of at least 0.80. We present a sample of 177 of these tasks as examples that show the breadth of tasks the model can complete. Performance varied systematically by outcome and clinical domain. Conclusions. PhenOM demonstrates the ability to complete thousands of predictive tasks across clinical domains and outcomes at the individual patient level, without additional training. Outcomes include screening for undiagnosed conditions, predicting future conditions, medical events, effects of treatments, and assessing care opportunities. These can be ascertained at the individual patient and population levels. These findings support applications in individual and population health management, risk management, drug development, and real-world evidence generation, and establish a transparent, reproducible performance reference for a large-scale real-world predictive AI platform.

title: Ultrasound-Based Precision Assessment and Intervention of Vulnerable Atherosclerotic Plaques: From Plaque Characterization to Therapeutic Modulation
authors: Yang Sun; Wang Luo; Zhang Qun-xia; Jianli Ren; Zhigang Wang; Haitao Ran
journal: Advanced ultrasound in diagnosis and therapy
abstract: Abstract Luminal stenosis remains central to clinical decision-making but does not fully characterize the plaque features associated with instability and embolization. This narrative review examines the progression from ultrasound-based plaque characterization to therapeutic modulation, with carotid atherosclerosis as the principal clinical focus. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) has the strongest human evidence among advanced methods for microvascular plaque characterization, linking intraplaque enhancement with histologic neovascularization and symptomatic disease. Superb microvascular imaging, elastography, and ultrasound localization microscopy provide complementary measures of slow flow, tissue mechanics, and microvascular architecture. Molecular ultrasound has visualized endothelial activation, platelet deposition, and angiogenic targets in animal models; studies of human endarterectomy specimens have confirmed the expression and accessibility of several candidate vascular targets ex vivo. Experimental nanoscale probes also target foam-cell lipids and extracellular matrix within plaque. Ultrasound-targeted delivery and sonodynamic therapy (SDT) modify macrophages, matrix, and neovessels in experimental plaques. A randomized SDT trial in femoropopliteal disease reported reduced plaque inflammation and improved walking performance; small carotid or mixed-territory studies report imaging responses. Carotid stroke-prevention benefit remains to be established. Serial ultrasound measurements during lipid-lowering treatment provide a human application of imaging-based response assessment.

title: Metainflammation and autonomic instability in the genesis of anxiety
authors: Milica Borovčanin; Branislav Milovanović; Nikola Markovic; Ivica Petrović
abstract: Anxiety is a complex condition that encompasses a range of mental disorders. It can manifest as a core symptom in various neurotic disorders, including anticipatory anxiety, pervasive anxiety, panic attacks, obsessive-compulsive, conversion and somatoform disorders. Anxiety is often linked to autonomic instability, which can be both observed and felt subjectively. However, anxiety does not arise solely from mental disorders; it can also occur alongside somatic conditions related to autonomic instability and cardiorenometabolic syndrome. Obesity and cardiorenometabolic syndrome, which can lead to diabetes and are associated with metainflammation, represent significant societal challenges that adversely impact mental functioning. In this context, neuroinflammation should be viewed as a consequence within the central nervous system of systemic inflammation and may be related to anxiety. Anti-inflammatory strategies have been shown to stabilize mental functioning, exhibit anxiolytic properties, and promote balance in the autonomic nervous system and metabolic homeostasis, with interconnected effects. While certain medications and procedures can influence these interrelated processes, they may also lead to undesirable side effects. This narrative review aims, for the first time, to jointly explore the triad of metainflammation, autonomic instability, and anxiety, in an attempt to clarify these important associations for future research and implementation in clinical practice.

title: Motion Picture
abstract: Aim: Degenerated valvular disease is more and more popular in the old patients.Traditional sternotomy cardiac operations have cause massive injury for these patients.To minimize the trauma, fullendoscopic cardiac operation is adopted via right mini-thoracotomy.Methods: The femoral vein and artery cannulations were placed guiding by transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) through this kind of peripheral cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB).Two small incisions were made in the parasternal 3rd intercostal for the main working port and camera.With the help of thoracoscope, surgeons used special instruments to conduct the valve maneuver.In this case, aortic valve was severely calcified, we carefully excised the valve to protect the aortic annulus.The residual calcified tissue were sucked preventing any embolism events.After sizing this patient's aortic annulus, 21 mm bioprosthesis valve was chosen, which was fit for her body surface area.We used continuous suture to implant the artificial bioprosthesis valve into the annulus, followed by the closure of the aortic wall.Results: In this very case, patient receive the bioprosthesis valve replacement through mini-incisions thoracotomy, which was successfully done uneventfully guiding by thoracoscope.Patient was discharged at the 8th day after the operation.Conclusion: In old patients, this full-endoscopic surgery could be applied in degenerated valvular disease.This kind of minimal-invasive operation could be completed and used in larger amount of patients.

title: Clinical outcomes of total endovascular aortic arch repair by in situ microneedle fenestration using the triple (stiff)-sheathed gutter technique
authors: 叶鹏; Hongfei Miao; Qingle Zeng; Wenya Liu; Mingyuan Ma; Yong Chen
abstract: PURPOSE: To investigate the outcomes of total endovascular aortic arch repair (TEAAR) via in situ micro-needle fenestration (ISMNF) with the triple (stiff)-sheathed gutter technique. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this retrospective study, the data of consecutive patients who underwent TEAAR via ISMNF with triple (stiff)-sheathed gutter technique between August 2022 and April 2025 were analyzed. Three 6-Fr, 90-cm sheaths were placed into ascending aorta without removing the dilator and super-stiff guidewires during main stent-graft deployment. This configuration creates a gutter between the stent-graft and aortic wall to maintain perfusion to supra-aortic branches. Operative details, technical success, 30-day and midterm outcomes, and adverse events were recorded. Kaplan-Meier analysis was used to estimate freedom from all-cause death and reintervention. RESULTS: Overall, 36 patients were included. The technical success rate was 94.4% (34/36). Endovascular reconstruction of cervical branches was successfully performed in all cases. The 30-day mortality was 2.8%. The median follow-up period was 19 months (range, 1-32 months). The all-cause death rate was 11.1% (4/36), with no cases of any aorta-related death. The prevalence of endoleaks during follow-up was 13.9% (5/36). The overall stroke rate was 8.3% (3/36). The 1- and 2-year survival rates were 97.3% ± 2.7% and 85.8% ± 8.1%, respectively. The cumulative rate of freedom from reintervention at 1 and 2 years was 87.5% ± 5.9% and 83.2% ± 7.0%, respectively. CONCLUSION: TEAAR via ISMNF with the triple (stiff)-sheathed gutter technique was performed with a 94% technical success rate and stroke risk similar to open surgery.

title: Endoscopic Lumbar Interbody Fusion Versus Minimally Invasive Transforaminal Lumbar Interbody Fusion: A Structured Debate and International Practice Patterns
authors: Win Boonsirikamchai; Khanathip Jitpakdee; Don Young Park; Zubair Khalid; Rizwan Akram; Ariel Matias Kaen; Christoph Johannes Laux; Ahmed Ibrahim; Akarawit Asawasaksakul; John Choi; Avelino Parajon; Asrafi Rizki Gatam; Xavier A. Santander; José Miguel Spirig; Koichi Sairyo; Alberto Ofenhejm Gotfryd; Mazda Farshad; Cheul Woong Park; Vit Kotheeranurak; Xuexiao Ma; Roger Härtl; Jae‐Joong Kim
abstract: Lumbar fusion has evolved from open transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) to minimally invasive TLIF (MIS-TLIF), the current minimally invasive benchmark. Endoscopic techniques, proven in discectomy and decompression, have been extended to fusion (uniportal endoscopic TLIF and biportal endoscopic TLIF), offering an alternative to MIS-TLIF. This structured debate-style review critically compares both techniques across 7 domains to clarify their respective roles in lumbar degenerative disease. It combined independent advocacy drafts with an international survey of 106 respondents across 35 countries, capturing procedural preferences and case-based reasoning. Using a prespecified 70% agreement threshold, domains were classified as domains with ≥70% panel agreement, whereas domains falling below this threshold were categorized as domains below the prespecified agreement threshold. This represents structured international survey agreement, not a formal Delphi process. Endoscopic fusion offers advantages in decreased blood loss, soft-tissue preservation, early postoperative back pain, and early recovery, with comparable mid-term clinical outcomes (long-term insufficiently established) to MIS-TLIF, which remains more reproducible and familiar. Complication rates are similar but technique-sensitive for endoscopic fusion. Panel responses favored endoscopic approaches for morbidity-related domains (soft-tissue preservation 89.6%, visualization 81.1%, recovery 74.5%), while fusion stability, short- to mid-term clinical outcomes, complications, and revision remained context-dependent without clear agreement. Endoscopic fusion is a credible option for selected single-level lumbar degenerative disease, offering perioperative advantages with comparable mid-term outcomes to MIS-TLIF; core endpoints, including fusion rate and revision rate, did not reach 70% panel agreement, even among endoscopy-favorable panelists. MIS-TLIF retains reproducibility advantages. The debate has shifted from feasibility to implementation, training standardization, cost-effectiveness, and long-term durability.

title: Myocardial remodelling during sacubitril/valsartan therapy in patients with chronic heart failure.
authors: DAVID TABUKASHVILI; V. Kapetivadze; Tamar Lazashvili; Zviadi Maglaperidze
abstract: Abstract: The aim of the study was to identify differences between aliskiren and sacubitril/valsartan in their ability to influence cardiac remodelling, metabolic balance, neurohumoral activation, and clinical symptom severity. A comparative assessment of the clinical effectiveness and impact on the structural and functional state of the myocardium was conducted for two therapeutic strategies in patients with chronic heart failure in Georgia over a 12-month follow-up. The results demonstrated fundamentally different trajectories of therapeutic response. In the sacubitril/valsartan group, early clinical improvement was observed by 6 months, including significant reductions in systolic blood pressure (-6.2%, p<0.001), respiratory rate (-4.5%, p<0.001), and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide levels (-10.0%, p<0.05), along with improved oxygen saturation (+3.5%, p<0.001). Left ventricular ejection fraction increased significantly already at 6 months (from 34.2±4.7% to 37.4±4.0%, p<0.001) and further at 12 months (40.5±3.5%, p<0.001), accompanied by rapid improvement in New York Heart Association functional class, with 9.3% of patients achieving New York Heart Association I by study end. In contrast, the aliskiren group exhibited slower but more pronounced structural reverse remodelling. Significant reductions in left ventricular end-systolic volume (-15.8%, p=0.009), end-diastolic volume (-17.6%, p=0.016), and end-systolic diameter (p=0.002) were observed only at 12 months, along with a modest but significant increase in ejection fraction (p=0.030). Regression of functional mitral and tricuspid regurgitation and a significant decrease in pulmonary artery systolic pressure (-19.7%, p<0.05) were more prominent in this group. Both therapies led to significant improvements in carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, including reductions in glycated haemoglobin, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and triglycerides (p<0.05 for all), indicating a favourable systemic metabolic effect. Overall, findings suggest that sacubitril/valsartan may be preferable when rapid clinical stabilization is required, whereas aliskiren may represent an effective therapeutic option for patients with advanced structural cardiac remodelling.

title: Physiology-informed deep learning for early identification of sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy from echocardiographic cine loops: a multicenter development and external validation study
authors: Yuhan Zhao; Qinxue Wang; Jiawei Wang; Yi Han
abstract: Abstract Background Sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy (SICM) is heterogeneous and may involve abnormalities in cardiac contraction, relaxation, and beat-to-beat motion. Conventional echocardiographic measurements and cardiac troponin T (cTnT) may not fully capture dynamic changes in myocardial function during sepsis. We developed a physiology-informed deep-learning framework for early identification of SICM from apical four-chamber (A4C) echocardiographic cine loops. Methods Adult patients with sepsis were retrospectively identified from two centers. The first eligible A4C cine loop obtained within 24 h after sepsis onset was used for model development. SICM was defined by cardiac abnormalities observed during the septic episode. Cine loops were divided into physiologically aligned end-diastole-to-end-diastole cardiac cycles. The model combined EchoJEPA-based visual representation learning with phase-aware spatial and temporal modeling, LV area-derived physiological features, and multi-cycle aggregation. Internal validation was performed using patient-level grouped fivefold cross-validation. The final model was trained in the full development cohort and independently evaluated in MIMIC-IV-ECHO using a conventional cTnT-based SICM phenotype. Model performance was compared with direct EchoJEPA classification. Results The development cohort included 530 patients, including 305 with SICM and 225 sepsis-only controls. In patient-level grouped fivefold cross-validation, the physiology-informed model achieved an out-of-fold AUROC of 0.933 (95% CI, 0.910–0.954). The external cohort included 93 patients, including 39 with SICM and 54 sepsis-only controls. The model achieved an AUROC of 0.929 (95% CI, 0.864–0.980). The direct EchoJEPA baseline achieved an external AUROC of 0.735 (95% CI, 0.632–0.833). The paired difference in AUROC was 0.194 (95% CI, 0.095–0.294; DeLong test, P < 0.001). Results remained consistent in sensitivity analyses using alternative cTnT definitions. Conclusions A physiology-informed deep-learning framework enabled early identification of SICM from routinely acquired A4C cine loops and maintained discrimination in both internal cross-validation and an independent external cohort. Incorporating cardiac physiology into EchoJEPA improved discrimination compared with direct foundation-model classification. These findings support further prospective evaluation of physiology-informed echocardiographic video analysis for early identification of SICM.

title: Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest as the First Manifestation of ALCAPA in a 9-Week-Old Infant: Survival to Discharge After Emergency Repair and VA-ECMO
authors: Grzegorz Wróbel; Jakub Gruszka; Piotr Lewitowicz; Olga K. Adamczyk-Gruszka
abstract: Background and Clinical Significance: Anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA) usually presents with heart failure at 2–3 months of age; cardiac arrest as the first manifestation is rare and often recognized only at autopsy. Case Presentation: A previously healthy girl collapsed at home at 65 days of age. After dispatcher-assisted parental resuscitation, the emergency team found asystole and achieved return of spontaneous circulation after approximately 4 min of professional resuscitation; the total low-flow time was not recorded. She was in cardiogenic shock (left ventricular ejection fraction 19.8%, high-sensitivity troponin T 2620 ng/L) with acute kidney injury and coagulopathy consistent with disseminated intravascular coagulation. Echocardiography showed a dilated right coronary artery and no flow from the aorta into the left coronary artery. Emergency repair on day 1 was followed by venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) for 4 days and continuous renal replacement therapy. The Simpson ejection fraction reached about 50% by day 9, fell to 37–40% during respiratory deterioration and was 45–50% on day 27; mitral regurgitation, graded as massive during VA-ECMO, regressed to trace without valve surgery. She was discharged on day 42 with impaired diastolic indices; no formal neurological assessment was documented. Conclusions: ALCAPA should be considered in every infant with unexplained cardiac arrest, and post-resuscitation echocardiography should assess the coronary origins. Emergency repair with VA-ECMO can achieve survival to discharge despite multiorgan failure, but long-term cardiac and neurodevelopmental follow-up is required.

title: Nonischemic and normothermic beating cardiac xenotransplantation
authors: Daniel H. Wolbrom; Nobutoshi Matsumura; Morgan K. Moroi; Ishit Chauhan; Sho Fujiwara; Susan Qudus; Michael Brewer; Dilrukshi K. Ekanayake‐Alper; Dominik Hajosi; Lorne Schweitzer; Koji Takeda; Richard J. Levy; Stephan M. Juergensen; Oliver M. Barry; Miroslav Sekulic; David H. Sachs; Megan Sykes; Greg Nowak; Andrew Brooks Goldstone
abstract: Cardiac xenotransplantation—the transplantation of a heart from one species to another- offers a clinically viable solution to the organ shortage problem. Despite significant advances in genetic engineering technologies and new immunosuppressive medications such as co-stimulatory blockade, bringing cardiac xenotransplantation to the clinic still has several challenges. Perioperative cardiac xenograft dysfunction is a major limitation to long-term xenograft survival and is attributed to the ischemia-reperfusion damage associated with the procurement and transplant of the porcine heart. This dysfunction can be reduced by utilizing commercial ex vivo perfusion devices which limit the cold ischemia time. Unfortunately, these devices still require an obligatory ischemic period during the initial arrest with cardioplegia and subsequent explanting of the organ, and then again during the implantation of the heart. These commercial devices also do not support smaller pediatric sized hearts, reducing the pool of recipients eligible for xenografts. We sought to establish a novel method of explanting and orthotopically implanting beating donor hearts from genetically modified pigs without any ischemia, while maintaining normothermic perfusion in a pig-to-nonhuman primate model. Eliminating cold and warm ischemia has never previously been achieved in cardiac xenotransplantation and has important implications for bringing it to the clinic, as well as broader translatability in allotransplantation. We performed a proof-of-concept experiment utilizing our novel technique in a non-survival model and then performed a successful experiment with nearly 8 weeks of survival of a single GGTA1 knockout pig heart. Our initial data suggest that utilization of a normothermic coronary perfusion circuit in cardiac xenotransplantation is feasible and safe and may be a plausible method towards achieving survival.

title: Myoglobin-centred multimarker phenotyping of chronic heart failure: results of an unsupervised cluster analysis
authors: M. O. Kolotylo; O. V. Starostenko; Ievgenii Andrieiev; Л.В. Натрус
abstract: The aim – to identify laboratory-pathophysiological phenotypes of chronic heart failure (CHF) using unsupervised cluster analysis of plasma levels of myoglobin (Myo), N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1), haem oxygenase-1 (HO-1), soluble transferrin receptor 1 (sTfR1), and vasodilator-stimulated phosphoprotein (VASP), without using predefined grouping variables, and to assess the association of the identified phenotypes with clinical-etiological patient cohorts.Materials and methods. This prospective, single-center observational study included 123 patients with CHF of various etiologies, including combined and isolated aortic and mitral regurgitation, non-valvular CHF, and postoperative thromboembolic complications. Biomarker concentrations were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Following appropriate logarithmic transformation, the data were standardized as Z-scores. Hierarchical cluster analysis using Ward’s method and squared Euclidean distance, together with k-means clustering, was performed. Agreement between the clustering solutions was assessed using the adjusted Rand index.Results and discussion. Four laboratory-pathophysiological phenotypes were identified: the Myo–NT-proBNP injury and hemodynamic-overload phenotype (n=28), the antioxidant-adaptive phenotype (n=32), the low multimarker-burden phenotype (n=47), and the VASP–sTfR1 vascular-metabolic signaling phenotype (n=16). Agreement between Ward’s method and k-means clustering was moderate (ARI=0.434). The distribution of clinical-etiological cohorts across the phenotypes was statistically significant (Pearson’s χ2 = 79.371; df=12; Monte Carlo exact p<0.001; Cramer’s V = 0.464), but did not correspond to a «one etiology – one phenotype» model. The strongest association was observed between non-valvular CHF and the Myo–NT-proBNP injury and hemodynamic-overload phenotype: 22 patients from this cohort belonged to the injury and hemodynamic-overload phenotype. The hypothesized distinct thrombotic-injury profile was not confirmed.Conclusions. In CHF, myoglobin should be assessed not in isolation but as part of a multimarker panel reflecting hemodynamic stress, antioxidant response, tissue iron availability, and vascular-metabolic signaling. The etiology of CHF is associated with biomarker profiles but does not uniquely determine them. These pilot findings support the potential of multimarker phenotyping for personalized risk stratification in patients with CHF and require external validation.

title: Clinical Impact of Multiple‐Clip Implantation for Residual Mitral Regurgitation After Transcatheter Edge‐to‐Edge Repair
authors: Takashi Nagasaka; Vivek Patel; Kazuki Suruga; Hidemasa Shitan; Yuchao Guo; Ofir Koren; Alon Shechter; Dhairya Patel; Tarun Chakravarty; Aakriti Gupta; Hideki Ishii; Hasan Jilaihawi; Moody M. Makar; Mamoo Nakamura; Raj Makkar
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
abstract: Background Residual moderate or greater mitral regurgitation (MR) after transcatheter edge‐to‐edge repair is strongly associated with adverse clinical outcomes. However, the prognostic impact of implanting additional clips in patients with significant residual MR after the first clip remains uncertain. We evaluated the clinical and echocardiographic outcomes of multiple‐clip implantation for significant residual MR following placement of the initial clip. Methods We retrospectively evaluated 826 patients with moderate or greater residual MR on intraprocedural transesophageal echocardiography after placement of the first clip during transcatheter edge‐to‐edge repair at the Cedars‐Sinai Medical Center from 2014 to 2023. Patients were categorized into single‐clip (n=113) and multiple‐clip (n=713) groups. The primary end point was the composite of all‐cause mortality and heart failure hospitalization at 1 year. Results Procedural technical success and complication rates were comparable between groups. The multiple‐clip group demonstrated greater MR reduction and higher transmitral pressure gradients at discharge, 30 days, and 1 year. At 1 year, the composite end point occurred less frequently in the multiple‐clip group than in the single‐clip group (16.8% versus 29.2%; P =0.002), along with greater and more sustained improvement in New York Heart Association functional class. In subgroup analyses, multiple‐clip implantation consistently reduced major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with moderate as well as moderate–severe/severe residual MR. Conclusions In patients with significant residual MR after implanting the first clip, multiple‐clip implantation improved MR reduction and 1‐year outcomes without increasing complications. Even in moderate residual MR, additional clips were associated with more favorable clinical outcomes.

title: Familial severe non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy with coexisting likely pathogenic BAG3 and FLNC variants: a case report
authors: Wang Lili; Youcao Wang; Xiaodong Yao; Zhen Wang
abstract: Background Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is genetically heterogeneous. In severe non-ischemic DCM with familial clustering of heart-failure deaths, genetic testing and pedigree analysis may clarify etiology and guide cascade screening. Case presentation A 40-year-old woman presented with progressive dyspnea, chest tightness, and palpitations after an upper respiratory tract infection. Echocardiography showed severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction [left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) approximately 20%], left atrial enlargement, functional mitral regurgitation, and a small pericardial effusion. Serial cardiac troponin I and myocardial enzyme measurements remained within the reference ranges. Coronary angiography excluded obstructive coronary disease. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) demonstrated global left ventricular hypokinesis and a clinically reported non-ischemic late-gadolinium-enhancement pattern at the papillary-muscle level involving the anterior/lateral wall. Because cardiac biomarkers remained normal and dedicated inflammatory CMR sequences were not acquired, active myocarditis could not be confirmed. Guideline-directed therapy reduced NT-proBNP from 4154 to 828 pg/mL, although angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor therapy was limited by symptomatic hypotension. At 2 months, symptoms and daily activity tolerance improved, but LVEF remained 25%, QTc was 479 ms, and ventricular premature complexes persisted. Whole-exome sequencing identified heterozygous likely pathogenic variants in BAG3 (NM_004281.4:c.180 + 1G > T) and FLNC [NM_001458.5:c.761_779del, p.(Leu254Profs*14)]. The daughter carried the BAG3 variant, whereas both children were negative for FLNC. The proband reported heart-failure-related deaths in her father and younger brother during adulthood and in a nephew during childhood. Conclusions The findings support complex familial non-ischemic DCM with marked variable expressivity. Coexisting BAG3 and FLNC variants should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than proof of dual-gene causality. The infection-associated acute decompensation, persistently normal cardiac injury biomarkers, non-ischemic LGE, and incomplete inflammatory CMR characterization favor cautious interpretation rather than a definitive diagnosis of myocarditis. Serial imaging, rhythm surveillance, individualized device-risk assessment, and follow-up of genotype-positive relatives are essential.

title: Atrial functional mitral regurgitation – current concepts in mechanisms, imaging, and management
authors: Marinka Peneva; Krasimir R. Dzhinsov; Tchavdar Nikolov Shalganov
abstract: Atrial functional mitral regurgitation (AF-MR) has emerged as a distinct subtype of secondary mitral regurgitation (MR) in the context of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and atrial ﬁ brillation, indicating advanced left atrial disease. This review outlines current knowledge in terms of pathophysiology, diagnosis, and therapy and highlights areas for further research. The differentiation between AF-MR and ventricular functional MR (VF-MR), primarily attributed to left ventricular (LV) remodeling, has important pathophysiological, diagnostic and treatment implications. Three-dimensional (3D) echocardiography and atrial function assessment have enabled detailed characterization of the underlying mechanism and guidance of treatment of AF-MR. Integrated therapeutic management ranges from optimal medical therapy for HFpEF, catheter ablation (CA), mitral valve annuloplasty or transcatheter edge-to-edge repair. AF-MR is a distinct disease with growing signiﬁcance driven by left atrial cardiomyopathy. The combination of advanced imaging, optimal medical therapy, and interventional strategies may improve prognosis. More detailed research in patient selection and timing of intervention is required to facilitate clinical outcomes.

title: Clozapine-Induced Myocarditis: Two Case Reports From Korea
authors: Jeonghoon Lee; Sungchul Cho; Nuree Kang; Se Hyun Kim
abstract: Clozapine is a highly effective antipsychotic, but its use is limited by potentially fatal adverse reactions. People of Asian ancestry have a higher risk of clozapine-induced inflammatory complications, yet reports of clozapine-induced myocarditis (CIM) in this population remain scarce. We present two cases of CIM from a Seoul National University Hospital cohort. Both were young Korean males with schizophrenia spectrum disorders undergoing clozapine titration along with concomitant valproic acid and olanzapine. Eleven days after clozapine initiation, both patients developed spiking fevers with elevations in inflammatory markers and cardiac enzymes; subsequently, they developed more severe symptoms, such as dyspnea, chest pain, and altered mentality. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia, and echocardiography revealed decreased systolic function. After clozapine discontinuation, symptoms and abnormalities in laboratory markers and electrocardiography resolved. These cases illustrate the clinical course of CIM in Asian young males and highlight the importance of monitoring inflammatory markers during clozapine titration.

title: Clinical profile, complications, and factors associated with mortality among children with rheumatic mitral stenosis in a resource-limited setting: a retrospective cohort study
authors: Ezra Fantahun Girmay¹; Tedros Hailu Abay; Marta Yemane Hadush; Mohammed Mustefa Mohammedamin; Yonas Moges Legese; Dawit Yemane Arefayine¹; Zeray Welegebrieal Marru; Alemseged Berhane Tesfa
abstract: Abstract Background Rheumatic mitral stenosis (MS) is an important cause of morbidity and mortality among children in low-resource settings. In Tigray, Ethiopia, cardiac surgical and catheter-based interventions are unavailable, and the clinical profile and outcomes of pediatric MS are poorly characterized. We assessed the clinical characteristics, complications, and factors associated with mortality among children with rheumatic MS. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study at Ayder Comprehensive Specialized Hospital, a tertiary referral center. We used records of children younger than 18 years with echocardiographically confirmed rheumatic MS diagnosed between April 2019 and April 2024. Ninety-eight children were included. Data were abstracted using a structured tool and analyzed with SPSS version 27 and R version 4.6.1. Factors associated with documented mortality were examined using univariable and multivariable Firth penalized logistic regression (logistf package); p < 0.05 was considered significant. Complications were coded as present if documented at any time during follow-up, and MS severity was taken from the last available echocardiogram. Results Mean age at diagnosis was 13.7 ± 3.0 years (youngest, 5 years). On the last echocardiogram, 59 children (60.2%) had severe MS. Heart failure was documented in 84.7%, and 61 of 75 children with available peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity (TR Vmax) measurements (81.3%) had a high echocardiographic probability of pulmonary hypertension. Moderate-to-severe thinness and stunting were present in 75.5% and 52.0% of children, respectively. Sixteen children (16.3%) died. Atrial fibrillation (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] 8.35; 95% CI 1.64–45.78; p = 0.011) and peripheral edema (AOR 4.77; 95% CI 1.35–17.86; p = 0.016) were associated with higher adjusted odds of mortality. Infective endocarditis showed a positive but non-significant association (AOR 4.72; 95% CI 0.91–22.80; p = 0.064). Conclusions In this tertiary-referral cohort without access to valve intervention, rheumatic MS in children was often severe on the last echocardiogram and accompanied by a high burden of malnutrition, complications, and mortality. Atrial fibrillation and peripheral edema were associated with higher odds of documented mortality in an exploratory model based on 16 deaths. The timing of these findings relative to death was unknown, so causal or prognostic effects cannot be inferred. Early detection, nutritional support, and access to definitive intervention merit attention.

title: Can the QTc interval and T-wave morphology change intermittently in arrhythmogenic mitral valve prolapse? First paediatric case experience
authors: Senem Özgür; Serpil Kaya Çelebi; Selman Kesici; Murat Akkuş; Yakup Ergül
abstract: BACKGROUND: Mitral valve prolapse is typically considered a benign condition. However, a newly described repolarisation anomaly known as arrhythmogenic mitral valve prolapse syndrome is closely associated with repolarisation disturbances and can potentially lead to sudden cardiac death. Arrhythmogenic mitral valve prolapse syndrome is characterised by bileaflet mitral valve prolapse, mitral valve regurgitation, T-wave inversions in the inferolateral leads, and complex ventricular ectopy. CASE REPORT: In this case, we present the diagnosis of arrhythmogenic mitral valve prolapse syndrome in a 16-year-old adolescent girl who experienced sudden cardiac arrest during exercise. Her electrocardiograms revealed intermittent QT/QTc prolongation. Interestingly, QT prolongation was always associated with T wave inversion in inferolateral leads. Heterozygous genomic changes were detected in the KCNH2 gene and the 25th exon of the ANK2 gene. These findings support the diagnosis of arrhythmogenic mitral valve prolapse syndrome in this patient. CONCLUSIONS: Since mitral valve prolapse is a common condition in the society, it is important to determine beforehand which ones are at risk of sudden death. As these boundaries are drawn better, underdiagnosis as well as overdiagnosis will be prevented.

title: A Rare Case Report of Type II Kounis Syndrome With Literature Review: Acute Anterior ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction Following Bee Sting
authors: Sara Tarkiani; Mobina Ghajar; Mohammad Hossein Sharifi Fard; Mohammad Ghasemi Palangi; Armin Bordbar; Hassan Ahangar; Amin Ramezani
abstract: Kounis syndrome (KS), also known as allergic angina, is a rare but serious condition defined by acute coronary syndrome occurring alongside a hypersensitivity reaction. We report the case of a 42-year-old male smoker who developed Type II KS after a hymenoptera sting. The patient came to the emergency department with a sudden decreased level of consciousness and retrosternal chest pain. Electrocardiography showed ST-segment elevation in the anterior leads, and coronary angiography revealed total proximal left anterior descending artery occlusion. Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) was performed successfully. Echocardiography documented a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 35% with regional wall motion abnormalities, indicating significant myocardial injury. The patient was discharged with a treatment plan that included valsartan, spironolactone, bisoprolol, ticagrelor, acetylsalicylic acid, and atorvastatin. This case highlights the diagnostic and treatment challenges of KS and stresses the need for early recognition and a team-based approach to achieve better clinical results.

title: Long-term outcomes of post-infarction aneurysm repair and preoperative prediction for left ventricular resection: A non-randomized retrospective cohort study
authors: Natalia I. Fedoseeva; Leonid N. Ivanov; Lev A. Leifer; Yuri V. Shcherbatov; П. Н. Кордатов; Lyudmila N. Antsygina
abstract: Background. Reverse left ventricular remodeling is a process characterized by a reduction in cardiac chamber volume and the restoration of normal ventricular geometry. These structural changes enhance myocardial systolic and diastolic function, specifically improving the heart’s ability to efficiently fill and eject blood. However, some patients may still experience the clinical progression of circulatory insufficiency. Postoperative reverse cardiac remodeling is influenced by optimal therapy, coronary revascularization, left ventricular aneurysm repair, mitral regurgitation correction, and cardiac resynchronization therapy. Objective. To evaluate surgical outcomes in patients with post-infarction left ventricular aneurysms and to develop an artificial intelligence model for predicting postoperative echocardiographic parameters across different follow-up periods. Methods. This non-randomized retrospective cohort study evaluated 130 patients with post-infarction left ventricular aneurysms who had undergone the Dor procedure and coronary artery bypass grafting. The surgeries were performed at the Research Institute – Specialized Cardiac Surgery Clinical Hospital Named after Academician B.A. Korolev in 2011–2021. The primary study endpoints included the predictors of complications associated with hemodynamic correction during both the early and long-term postoperative follow-up, as well as the feasibility of using an artificial intelligence model (CatBoost) to determine the extent of left ventricular myocardial resection. The model was trained using retrospective data on short- and long-term surgical outcomes. The following preoperative echocardiographic parameters served as predictors: end-diastolic volume, end-systolic volume, ejection fraction, and sphericity index. The target variables consisted of the same parameters recorded 7 days postoperatively. During training, optimal hyperparameter values were selected for each target variable to ensure the best predictive performance for Day 7. Similar models were constructed to predict outcomes at 3 and 6 months after surgery. Results. Preoperative echocardiography demonstrated that cardiac volumetric parameters were significantly elevated: end-diastolic volume was 169 [141–205] mL; end-systolic volume, 95[75–128] mL; ejection fraction, reduced to 41.7%; and the sphericity index, elevated at 0.7 [0.7–1]. These data indicate initial signs of left ventricular remodeling. The study showed a statistically significant reduction in left ventricular volumetric parameters in patients during both the early and long-term postoperative follow-up. The artificial intelligence model (CatBoost) yielded a low median prediction error (20%) for the estimated cardiac parameters compared to actual values. This demonstrates high accuracy of the model, as well as its potential clinical utility for surgical planning and complication risk reduction. Conclusion. During long-term postoperative follow-up, patients exhibited significant reverse left ventricular remodeling, as evidenced by positive changes in volumetric parameters and ejection fraction. This predictive model constitutes a promising tool for preoperative planning, specifically for optimizing surgical techniques and reducing the risk of low cardiac output syndrome.

title: Percutaneous Intramyocardial Septal Radiofrequency Ablation (Liwen Procedure) for Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: A Decade of Evolution, Clinical Experience and Future Perspectives
authors: Liwen Liu; Jing Li; Shaonan Dang; David H. Hsi; Shengjun Ta
journal: Advanced ultrasound in diagnosis and therapy
abstract: Abstract Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is an inherited cardiomyopathy. For patients with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (oHCM) who remain symptomatic despite medical therapy, septal reduction therapy can be performed. Surgical septal myectomy and alcohol septal ablation are the treatments for relieving left ventricular outflow tract obstruction and can effectively improve patients’ quality of life. In recent years, percutaneous intramyocardial septal radiofrequency ablation (PIMSRA/Liwen procedure) has emerged as a novel treatment for oHCM. This review traces its ten-year development from animal experiments to clinical application, covering technical principles, safety, and efficacy. Additional potentially extended applications are being explored, including non-obstructive HCM and other coexisting cardiac conditions. Future directions include longer-term follow-up, and multicenter collaboration to validate efficacy and safety in HCM patients. This review summarizes the current knowledge on PIMSRA/Liwen procedure and raises several issues that deserve further investigation.

title: Integrating tissue proteomics and bioactive lipid analysis of ovine tissue samples identifies functional relations of bioactive lipids
authors: Gerhard Hagn; Florien Jenner; Andrea Bileck; Sinan Gültekin; Mats Hámberg; Thomas T. Mohr; Christopher Gerner; Iris Gerner
abstract: Bioactive lipids are potent effector molecules that may help to reveal specific information about biological processes. However, analytical challenges and incomplete functional annotations remain as obstacles. We hypothesized that the functional annotation of these lipids may be improved by projecting enriched Gene Ontology (GO) terms derived from proteomics to correlating bioactive lipids. To that aim, thirteen organs and tissues from sheep ( Ovis aries ) were analyzed using mass spectrometry-based untargeted proteomics and bioactive lipid analysis. In total, 4717 proteins and 168 bioactive lipids, including fatty acids and their conjugates, oxylipins (octadecanoids, eicosanoids, and docosanoids), lyso-phosphatidylcholines (LPCs) and lyso-phosphatidylethanolamines (LPEs), endocannabinoids and related fatty amides, and bile acids and related sterol lipids were determined. Thereof, the correct identification of 114 lipids was confirmed using commercially available analytical standards, whereas the identity of the previously uncharacterized oxylipin 4-hydroxy-eicosatetraenoic acid (4-HETE) was verified through in-house chemical synthesis. Co-expression and clustering analyses are consistent with our hypothesis via independently corroborating known bioactive lipid functions and suggested novel functional relations. Amongst other observations, 18-HETE and 19-HETE were related to mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation, 11,12-dihydroxy-eicosatetraenoic acid (DiHETE), 15-deoxy-prostaglandin J2 and 5(6)-epoxy-eicosatrienoic acid (EET) were related to chemical synaptic transmission, arachidonoyl ethanolamide phosphate was related to muscle contraction and numerous LPCs and LPEs were related to exosome formation. Tissue levels of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), pro-resolving mediators and the newly characterized 4-HETE were related to the cellular protein synthesis and folding machinery. The latter finding suggested that PUFAs and their derivatives support protein synthesis fidelity in addition to efferocytosis, both essential contributors for the effective resolution of inflammation.

title: High Rates of Atrial Fibrillation among Inpatients with Heart Failure or Ischemic Stroke in Southwestern Uganda
authors: Peter Olds; Precious Twesigye; Lydia Nakawesa; Ivan Kasomba; Jessica Elizabeth Haberer; Abeya Fardous
abstract: Background: Atrial fibrillation (AF) affects over 37 million people worldwide, and its prevalence is projected to increase by 60% by 2050. Addressing AF is critical in Uganda and elsewhere in sub‑Saharan Africa, where data are lacking despite the high prevalence of AF risk factors, comorbidities, and sequelae. Objectives: To evaluate AF prevalence among inpatients with acute heart failure or acute ischemic stroke in Uganda. Methods: Between November 4, 2024 and November 30, 2025, we recruited a cohort of inpatients at the Regional Referral Hospital in Mbarara, Uganda with either acute heart failure or acute ischemic stroke. We collected baseline clinical data and hospital outcomes, performed a transthoracic echocardiogram, and equipped participants with a 24‑hour Holter monitor. A multivariable logistic regression model was fitted for a primary outcome of AF detection. Results: Among 250 individuals, mean age was 61.7 years (SD 20.5), of whom 175 (70.0%) were women. 123 (49.2%) had acute heart failure; 127 (50.8%) had acute ischemic stroke. Holter monitors detected AF in 105 (42.0%), with a mean AF duration of 11.0 hours (IQR 1.0–21.9) with a bimodal distribution. Mean stroke risk (CHA2DS2VA) was 3.5 (SD 1.6). Factors associated with AF included increasing age in years (OR 1.04, 95% CI 1.02–1.06) and left atrial volume index (mL/m2) (OR 1.02, 95% CI 1.01–1.03). Conclusions: We found high rates of AF among inpatients with acute heart failure or acute ischemic stroke, comparable to studies from the United States and Europe. These findings highlight the need to address AF in Uganda, with improved screening using long‑term monitors, updated treatment protocols, and broadened access to cardiac care.
